purpose: Find original NSEP questions about E=K+U constant, E>=U and turning positions E=U, K=0; no authored assessment questions.

copyright_and_source_custody.reason: Original exam PDF wording is copyrighted; supply source-exact official paper links, printed page and question locators instead of reproducing long stems/options or inventing them. Authored short synopses are not questions.

original.non_verbatim_indexing_synopsis: Initially a spring is compressed by a constant force F to a distance ξ; the force is suddenly reversed and doubled; find the farthest extension beyond natural length.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Select a post-reversal effective potential for spring plus applied constant force, rather than spring potential alone.

representation_translation.evidence: Convert compression and extension into signed positions x = −ξ and x > 0.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: First infer kξ=F, then set the post-switch conserved energy, then locate the other rest position.

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Expand and factor a quadratic in x/ξ.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: A changed applied force invalidates conservation of spring energy alone; the −2Fx contribution is decisive.

labelling.difficulty_reason: Score 7: switching the force changes the appropriate potential, and a second turning root must be selected.
labelling.key_step: Choose x positive along the new applied force, so the initial coordinate is −ξ; after switching, U_eff(x)=kx²/2−2Fx.
hint_ladder_authored_not_source: Decide what happens to the conserved energy expression immediately after the force changes.
Measure x from natural length; compression and extension have opposite signs.
At the extreme extension, speed is again zero; compare the total potential at the two rest points.

reasoning_route.description: At the initial equilibrium the original force gives F=kξ.
Choose x positive along the new applied force, so the initial coordinate is −ξ; after switching, U_eff(x)=kx²/2−2Fx.
Immediately after switching the spring is still at −ξ with zero speed: E= kξ²/2+2Fξ=5kξ²/2.
At an extreme extension K=0, hence kx²/2−2kξx=5kξ²/2.
Thus x²−4ξx−5ξ²=(x−5ξ)(x+ξ)=0; exclude the already-known initial root x=−ξ.
The other turning point is x=5ξ, choice d.

answer.writer_solution: Use F=kξ. A constant force of magnitude 2F directed toward extension has potential −2Fx. Conservation after the switch is (k/2)x²−2kξx=(5/2)kξ² at the two zero-velocity points. Factoring yields x=−ξ (starting point) and x=5ξ (maximum extension). Therefore d.

original.figure_exact_visual_description: A single uniform chain is drawn as open oval links lying horizontally across a frictionless tabletop, bending around the rounded right edge and hanging vertically. A vertical line marks the edge; a downward arrow on the hanging side is labelled y. No masses or angles are separately marked.
original.non_verbatim_indexing_synopsis: A uniform flexible chain (length L, mass/length λ) starts stationary with hanging length y₀ over a smooth table edge; obtain its speed when fully vertical.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Recognise a constant-mass chain as one energy-conserving system despite changing hanging mass.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate changing dangling length into gravitational energy of a uniform segment at centre-of-mass depth y/2.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Form U_initial and U_final, calculate their difference, and equate to whole-chain kinetic energy.

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Simplify λg(L²−y₀²)/2 against the kinetic energy λLv²/2.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: The hanging segment alone does not supply the complete kinetic mass; all of λL moves.

labelling.difficulty_reason: Score 7: distributed gravitational energy and all-chain kinetic energy must be coordinated.
labelling.key_step: When length y hangs, that portion has mass λy and mean gravitational height −y/2; therefore U(y)=−λgy²/2.
prerequisites: centre of mass of a uniform straight segment at its midpoint
mechanical energy conservation on a frictionless surface
all chain links have the same speed
hint_ladder_authored_not_source: Use the tabletop edge as zero gravitational height.
At a hanging length y, determine the hanging mass and its centre-of-mass depth.
For kinetic energy, remember the entire chain is moving when it leaves the table.

reasoning_route.description: When length y hangs, that portion has mass λy and mean gravitational height −y/2; therefore U(y)=−λgy²/2.
The initial energy is E_i=−λgy₀²/2 because the chain is released from rest.
Just before leaving the edge, U_f=−λgL²/2 and K_f=(λL)v²/2.
Set E_i=U_f+K_f and cancel λ/2.
Obtain Lv²=g(L²−y₀²), hence v=√[g(L−y₀²/L)], choice a.

answer.writer_solution: Take the table-edge height as U=0. The initial dangling segment has mass λy₀ and its centre of mass lies y₀/2 below the edge, so U_i=−λgy₀²/2. The final chain has mass λL and COM L/2 below the edge, so U_f=−λgL²/2. Thus (λL)v²/2=λg(L²−y₀²)/2. Divide through: v²=g(L−y₀²/L), giving a.

source.official_key_kind: IAPT official published worked solution with explicit Ans field

original.non_verbatim_indexing_synopsis: A particle is released from rest at x₀=α/β in U(x)=α/x²−β/x for α,β>0. Test four claims about rewriting U, finding v(x), maximum speed and total mechanical energy.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Apply a single conserved energy to all four statements, identifying E=U(x₀)=0.

representation_translation.evidence: Introduce dimensionless z=x₀/x and preserve the admissible interval 0≤z≤1 implied by E≥U.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Coordinate potential rescaling, energy conservation, velocity expression, domain and maximum-speed evaluation.

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Symbolically substitute β=α/x₀, solve for square-root velocity and complete a square to maximise z−z².

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: A positive kinetic energy coexists with E=0 because U can be negative; the x-domain cannot be ignored.

labelling.difficulty_reason: Score 8: several symbolic conclusions depend on one conserved-energy invariant and careful domain handling.
labelling.key_step: At the release point x=x₀, U(x₀)=0 and K=0; thus the conserved total energy E=0.
prerequisites: inequalities and position domains; calculus not required
hint_ladder_authored_not_source: Find the starting value of potential energy before writing the speed formula.
Express U in terms of the dimensionless ratio x₀/x.
A quadratic of the form z−z² has a maximum that can be found by completing the square.

reasoning_route.description: Since x₀=α/β, write β=α/x₀ and U(x)=α/x₀²[(x₀/x)²−x₀/x].
At the release point x=x₀, U(x₀)=0 and K=0; thus the conserved total energy E=0.
Hence K(x)=−U(x)=α/x₀²[z−z²] where z=x₀/x, and v(x)=√{2α/[mx₀²]·[z−z²]}.
The accessible outward branch has x≥x₀ and thus 0<z≤1; x₀ is its finite turning point and no smaller positive x is accessible.
Complete the square z−z²=1/4−(z−1/2)²; its maximum 1/4 occurs at z=1/2 or x=2x₀.
Then v_max²=α/(2mx₀²). Claims a, b, c and d all hold.

answer.writer_solution: Substitute β=α/x₀. At release, U(x₀)=α/x₀²−α/x₀²=0, so E=K+U=0 for the motion. Set z=x₀/x: U=α(z²−z)/x₀² and v²=(2α/(mx₀²))(z−z²). Thus statements a, b and d are true. For maximum speed, complete the square: z−z²=1/4−(z−1/2)²; maximum at z=1/2 (x=2x₀), giving v_max=√[α/(2mx₀²)]. Thus c true and official set a,b,c,d agrees. Motion on the positive axis cannot enter 0<x<x₀ because then U>0=E.

extra_knowledge_needed: Requires algebraic domain awareness beyond routine Grade 9; maximum is obtainable without differentiation.

original.figure_exact_visual_description: A thin vertical uniform rod OA is attached to a small pin pivot at top O with three short hatch strokes indicating support. Its midpoint is marked by a black dot labelled C, and the free lower endpoint is labelled A. There is no arrow or additional angular position drawn.
original.non_verbatim_indexing_synopsis: A rod of length L pivots at its end O, has midpoint C, and is considered under various oscillation, release and midpoint-break scenarios; assess statements on period, speed and post-break motion.

option_values_index_not_original_wording.b: from horizontal rest ω at vertical =√(3g/L)
option_values_index_not_original_wording.c: after impulse-free fracture at C, upper half rises to 60° from vertical
option_values_index_not_original_wording.d: lower half falls vertically while rotating about own centre

concept_model_selection.evidence: Choose rotational kinetic-energy model for the intact rod and separately model the upper-half pendulum after break.

representation_translation.evidence: Convert uniform rod geometry to gravitational centre-of-mass height changes and pivot inertias.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Obtain intact angular speed, partition instantaneous kinetic energy, then solve the subsequent upper-half turning angle.

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Several short inertia and energy substitutions with consistent lengths and masses.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: After break the lower fragment retains horizontal COM velocity; assuming it drops vertically makes d falsely plausible.

labelling.difficulty_reason: Score 8: transfer from one rigid-body system to a post-break subsystem and an impulse-free velocity condition.
labelling.key_step: When the upper piece reaches a turning angle θ, K=0 and its COM rises by (L/4)(1−cosθ). Set MgL/16=(MgL/8)(1−cosθ), obtaining θ=60°; this confirms c under the horizontal-release state.
hint_ladder_authored_not_source: For the intact rod, determine the height through which its centre of mass descends.
At the instant of a fracture without impulse, each piece keeps the instantaneous velocities it had just before breaking.
For the upper half, compare its rotational kinetic energy at the bottom with the gain in its centre-of-mass height at its furthest position.

reasoning_route.description: Let total rod mass be M. From horizontal rest, its COM descends L/2; equate MgL/2=(1/2)(ML²/3)ω².
This gives ω²=3g/L, confirming statement b.
Immediately after impulse-free fracture, the upper half has mass M/2, length L/2 and inertia about O: I_top=ML²/24.
At the break its kinetic energy about O is (1/2)I_topω²=MgL/16.
When the upper piece reaches a turning angle θ, K=0 and its COM rises by (L/4)(1−cosθ). Set MgL/16=(MgL/8)(1−cosθ), obtaining θ=60°; this confirms c under the horizontal-release state.
The physical pendulum period is 2π√[2L/(3g)], not the claim in a; the lower piece retains nonzero horizontal COM velocity and so does not fall strictly vertically, refuting d.

answer.writer_solution: For a uniform intact rod released from horizontal, E_g=M gL/2 goes into K_rot=(ML²/6)ω², so ω=√(3g/L) (b). If it breaks without impulse at the vertical, the attached top half has inertia (M/2)(L/2)²/3=ML²/24, with kinetic energy MgL/16. At its angular turning point: (M/2)g(L/4)(1−cosθ)=MgL/16, so cosθ=1/2 and θ=60° (c). Meanwhile a misstates the physical-pendulum period, and d overlooks the lower fragment’s horizontal COM velocity.

extra_knowledge_needed: Rotational energy, rotational inertia and physical-pendulum formula are beyond Grade 9 energy alone.
The interpretation of c uses the horizontal-release condition discussed in b; the standalone wording of c does not restate its starting amplitude.

original.figure_exact_visual_description: On a small rectangular graph, horizontal axis t(s) has labelled ticks 0,2,4,6,8,10; vertical axis x(cm) marks −15,−10,−5,0,5,10,15. A smooth nearly sinusoidal curve starts at (0,0) increasing, peaks near (2,5 cm), crosses zero near (4,0), reaches a trough near (6,−5 cm), crosses zero near (8,0), and rises to +5 cm near t=10 s. Axes form a boxed plot.
original.non_verbatim_indexing_synopsis: A sinusoidal position–time plot (x in cm versus t in s) for a 1 kg particle in a potential field is used to determine approximate total mechanical energy.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Identify near-sinusoidal motion and relate maximum speed to amplitude and period.

representation_translation.evidence: Extract amplitude and period from the plotted x–t curve and convert 5 cm to 0.05 m.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Determine frequency from graph, then use a maximum-speed relation before calculating energy.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: The energy reference must be taken at equilibrium and the centimetre-to-metre conversion affects the result by 10⁴.

labelling.difficulty_reason: Score 6: graph-to-physics translation and careful period, amplitude and units control the answer.
labelling.key_step: Use the SHM relation v_max=2πA/T=2π·0.05/8≈0.03927 m/s.
hint_ladder_authored_not_source: Read the time between successive peaks, not the time from the first crossing to a peak.
Convert graph amplitude to metres before using energy in joules.
At the equilibrium position the sinusoidal motion is fastest.

reasoning_route.description: Read amplitude A≈5 cm=0.05 m and period T≈8 s from peak-to-peak spacing.
Use the SHM relation v_max=2πA/T=2π·0.05/8≈0.03927 m/s.
With U=0 at equilibrium, E=K_max=(1/2)(1 kg)(0.03927 m/s)²≈7.71×10⁻⁴ J.
This corresponds to option c in the official final key.

answer.writer_solution: For a sinusoidal displacement of amplitude 0.05 m and period 8 s, the speed amplitude is ωA=(2π/8)·0.05=0.03927 m/s. Evaluating E=K_max=(1/2)(1)(0.03927)² gives 7.71×10⁻⁴ J, choice c. This is total mechanical energy only with the conventional equilibrium potential chosen as zero.

extra_knowledge_needed: Requires v_max=ωA for SHM, not derivable solely from E=K+U unless the potential model or SHM relation is supplied.
The exam gives no explicit potential-zero datum; official value presumes U_equilibrium=0.

rejected_candidates.reason: Maximum spring compression is a relative-coordinate turning point while the blocks retain common translational kinetic energy. Collisions, momentum and reduced-mass oscillation period are extra; distracts from K_total=0 at a one-particle turning point. Official b,d; not selected.

Potential U(x)=−100x/(x²+4) is tested mainly by force differentiation, equilibrium stability and small-oscillation frequency. Requires derivatives, not primarily WEP-07 conservation/turning; official a,b,c.
A potential-versus-position graph primarily asks for corresponding force plot via F=−dU/dx. WEP-07 E≥U and turning points are not the decisive act; official d.
Source has a force graph and asks for potential-energy properties, requiring force-to-potential area methods; not a direct conservation/turning-point item.
